learningObjective: Explain Ansor's central design choice of subgraph-level schedule generation with a learned cost model, and what it replaces.
stem: The Ansor paper (OSDI 2020) makes several design choices that distinguish it from prior work like AutoTVM and Halide autoscheduler. Which best describes Ansor's central design intent?

options.text: Ansor searches at the level of algorithmic sketches over multi-op subgraphs, uses a learned cost model to prune candidates, and prioritizes subgraphs by their contribution to end-to-end network runtime; this removes the need for per-operator manual templates while remaining tractable via the sketch abstraction.
Ansor is a compiler backend for CUDA that replaces cuBLAS and cuDNN with hand-written Tensor Core kernels; its main contribution is a superior tensor core code generator.
Ansor is a runtime autotuning framework that mutates kernel launch parameters between forward passes during model serving.
Ansor is a rewrite of AutoTVM's cost model in C++; the design intent is faster compile time at the cost of tuning quality.

explanation: Ansor's contributions per the OSDI 2020 paper are (i) hierarchical sketch generation that composes algorithmic templates automatically, (ii) evolutionary search + learned cost model, and (iii) task scheduler that prioritizes subgraphs by their contribution to end-to-end network runtime. The result is a system that discovers schedules for new operators without per-op templates. Option B misrepresents Ansor as a Tensor Core code generator. Option C misrepresents it as a runtime autotuner. Option D is a straw-man reimplementation claim.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches the paper's abstract and design overview.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Ansor is a scheduler generator, not a Tensor Core code generator.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Ansor operates at compile time, not per-serving-request.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: Ansor is a new architecture, not a C++ port of AutoTVM.

assumptions: The reader has knowledge of the Ansor paper's abstract-level contributions.
nonImplications: Does not imply Ansor supplants library kernels — high-quality library GEMMs often remain preferable.
Does not imply the task scheduler solves all tuning-budget issues — resource allocation across many subgraphs is still an approximation.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses Ansor with a CUDA library.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses Ansor with a runtime autotuner.
distractorRationales.D: Reduces Ansor to an implementation port.
